title: Citadel Buys Aschenbrenner's AI Fund Portfolio After 1,000% Gains Unravel
excerpt: Ken Griffin's hedge fund acquired most of Situational Awareness's public stocks after leverage amplified losses in the tech selloff, ending the most watched rise in AI investing.
body:
• Citadel, Ken Griffin's $71 billion hedge fund, has acquired the bulk of Situational Awareness's public stock portfolio after the AI-focused fund suffered heavy losses in the recent tech selloff.
  • Founded by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, 24, Situational Awareness had delivered a 439% return through June before leverage amplified its losses in July.
  • The fund still holds roughly $10 billion in assets, including its stake in Anthropic, but was forced to unwind leveraged public equity positions.
  • Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Citigroup facilitated the deal.

From 1,000% Returns to Forced Selling

It was the most spectacular rise in hedge fund history — and one of the swiftest reversals. Citadel, the $71 billion hedge fund run by Ken Griffin, has purchased most of the public stock portfolio of Situational Awareness, the AI-focused fund founded by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, after it was battered by heavy losses in tech stocks, according to Reuters, citing two sources familiar with the deal.

https://x.com/aakashgupta/status/2082892740485054786

Situational Awareness was forced to unwind most of its public equities portfolio, which included sizable positions in prominent AI names that have been hammered by the recent market selloff, including Broadcom, Intel, and CoreWeave. The fund had faced a choice: raise fresh capital from investors or offload its entire book. It chose the latter.

The Rise of a Wunderkind

Aschenbrenner, now 24, had no professional investing experience when he launched Situational Awareness in 2024 after being fired from OpenAI's superalignment team. His 165-page essay, also titled "Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead," predicted the trajectory of AI development with eerie precision and attracted a cult-like following among investors.

Early backers included Stripe co-founders Patrick and John Collison, along with Daniel Gross and Nat Friedman — both now leading Meta Platforms' AI efforts. Even Jane Street, the secretive quantitative trading firm that rarely allocates capital to outside managers, invested.

"We have not seen this level of attention on a hedge fund's filings in a very long time."

— John Coogan, TBPN podcast co-host

The fund's regulatory filings became events in themselves. The trading app Autopilot launched an option to copy Aschenbrenner's disclosed trades. When a filing revealed the fund had taken a stake in solar manufacturer T1 Energy, the stock surged 23% in a day.

Leverage Cuts Both Ways

Returns since inception had exceeded 1,000%, and assets under management had ballooned to around $20 billion, according to the Financial Times. But the same leverage that amplified gains during the AI boom compounded losses when the market turned.

Based on the fund's most recent SEC 13F filing from March, Situational Awareness held stakes in Bloom Energy, Riot Platforms, Nvidia, AMD, TSMC, Micron, Oracle, and Nebius, and was a cornerstone investor in SK Hynix's Nasdaq offering. When the Nasdaq 100 entered correction territory on fears that AI spending was outrunning returns, these positions were hit hard.

The Financial Times reported that Aschenbrenner had written to investors requesting fresh capital before ultimately choosing to sell. MarketWatch reported that Millennium Management had also bid on the portfolio.

What Remains

As part of the deal, Citadel is picking up the leveraged portion of Situational Awareness's public portfolio. The fund will retain roughly $10 billion in assets after the transaction, comprising stocks and private investments — most notably its stake in Anthropic, the AI lab backed by Amazon. Four major Wall Street prime brokers — Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Citigroup — helped facilitate the sale.

Some veteran investors had watched Aschenbrenner's rapid ascent with a mixture of envy and worry. The Wall Street Journal reported that concerns about a sudden collapse dragging down his concentrated stock positions had circulated for months.

Looking Ahead

The episode is a cautionary tale about leverage in concentrated portfolios, even when the underlying thesis proves directionally correct. Aschenbrenner's AI predictions have largely been validated — AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud are all reporting accelerating growth, and AI infrastructure spending continues to surge. But in markets, being right on the thesis and wrong on the timing or risk management can produce the same result: forced liquidation.

For the many Indian-origin professionals in AI and tech investing, Aschenbrenner's story resonates as both inspiration and warning. The AI trade is far from over, but its most aggressive bet just learned the oldest lesson on Wall Street.
nri_angle: The collapse of the most prominent AI-focused hedge fund is a cautionary tale for Indian-origin tech investors and professionals in the AI sector.
